content.text:
Yes — and for most of what you want, actual scraping is the wrong tool. Nearly every source worth having exposes an official API or a public git repo, which gets you full-resolution originals plus real license metadata, instead of thumbnails plus legal risk. Here's what I'd build.

## Where the assets actually come from

**Icons — git clone, not scraping.** These are all MIT/Apache/CC0 and ship as SVG source:

| Pack | License | Count |
|---|---|---|
| Iconify (unified API over ~150 sets) | per-set | 200k+ |
| Lucide / Feather | ISC / MIT | ~1,600 |
| Tabler | MIT | ~5,900 |
| Phosphor | MIT | ~9,000 (6 weights) |
| Heroicons | MIT | ~300 |
| Remix Icon | Apache 2.0 | ~3,000 |
| Material Symbols | Apache 2.0 | ~3,700 |
| Bootstrap Icons | MIT | ~2,000 |
| Simple Icons (brand logos) | CC0 | ~3,300 |

One `git clone` each gives you the whole pack, offline, versioned. Iconify's API covers the long tail on demand.

**Images — official APIs, free keys:** Unsplash, Pexels, Pixabay, Openverse (CC aggregator), Wikimedia Commons, plus pure public-domain museum/agency APIs (Met, Smithsonian, NASA). All return original resolution — Unsplash and Pexels are routinely 4000–6000px.

**Video — same story:** Pexels Videos and Pixabay Videos (both 1080p–4K, same keys as their image APIs), Coverr, NASA's library. Mixkit and Videvo have good free-license libraries but no API, so those are the only ones that would need real scraping — and Mixkit's terms forbid bulk downloading, so I'd skip them.

**Hard no:** Freepik, Flaticon, Envato, Shutterstock, Adobe Stock, Storyblocks, Artgrid. Their terms prohibit scraping and their assets aren't free for commercial use regardless of how the download link looks. Not worth it, and I won't build a scraper against them.

## The license catch worth knowing now

"Free for commercial use" universally means *use in your projects* — websites, videos, client work. It does **not** mean redistributing the assets as a pack. Unsplash and Pexels both explicitly forbid compiling their content into a competing library. So this vault is your private working library, not something to republish. Simple Icons is CC0 as code, but the logos are still trademarks — fine for "built with React," not for implying endorsement.

## What I'd build

A `tools/asset-vault/` alongside your existing `video-use` and `hyperframes`:

- **One fetcher per source**, keys in `.env`, rate-limited and resumable — kill it mid-run and restart without re-downloading.
- **A `manifest.json` ledger** per asset: source, ID, license, author, original URL, dimensions, duration, tags, SHA-256. This is what makes the vault usable a year from now instead of a folder of mystery MP4s, and it's also what keeps you clean if a client ever asks where a clip came from.
- **Quality gate on ingest** — reject below 1920×1080 for images, below 1080p for video, prefer 4K where offered.
- **Dedupe by perceptual hash**, since the same photo shows up across three aggregators.
- **Local search** over tags/colors/dimensions so a query returns paths, not a browser tab.

It'd mirror the ledger convention `/media-use` already uses, so resolved assets drop straight into HyperFrames compositions.

## Two things to decide before I start

**Storage** is the real constraint. Icons are trivial — all nine packs together are under 500MB. Images at ~5MB each: 5,000 photos ≈ 25GB. Video is the problem — 4K clips run 50–200MB, so 500 clips is 25–100GB. Your workspace is on OneDrive, which will try to sync all of it. I'd put the vault on a local non-synced path and symlink it in.

**Scope** — do you want a broad general library seeded by category (tech, nature, people, abstract, city), or targeted pulls per video project as you need them? The broad seed is a one-time overnight run; targeted keeps it small but means a fetch step in every project.

Tell me which way on both and I'll build it.

Good to know — I'll work from architecture rather than the local tree. From the folder contents, Nxeon looks like your own VPS/game-server hosting business (VPS panel, admin portal, onboarding screenshots), and Kodely is the Next.js + Prisma AI site builder. I skipped `nxeon root.txt` since it reads like server credentials.

Here's how I'd wire the two together.

## The one decision that drives everything else

Don't provision a VPS per customer. That's what Nxeon sells today, but it's the wrong unit for generated marketing sites — you'd be handing a dedicated vCPU to a five-page landing page, and you'd own OS patching for thousands of boxes.

Instead: **one shared edge tier on Nxeon, many sites behind it.** A couple of nodes running a reverse proxy, sites served from a content directory or object store, routed by `Host` header. That's how Vercel and Netlify work, and it's the difference between $0.05/site/month and $5.

Nxeon's VPS product stays as the upsell for customers who outgrow it.

## Architecture

```
Kodely (Next.js)  ──service API──>  Nxeon Control Plane  ──>  Edge nodes (Caddy)
      │                                    │                        │
   Postgres                          provisioning queue        site content
      │                                    │
   Stripe                          registrar + DNS APIs
```

**Nxeon exposes a service API that only Kodely calls** — not user-facing, authenticated with mTLS or HMAC-signed requests, never a key that ships to the browser:

| Endpoint | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/sites` | Create site, return `site_id` + `{slug}.kodely.app` |
| `POST /v1/sites/{id}/deployments` | Upload build tarball, atomic symlink swap, return deployment ID |
| `POST /v1/sites/{id}/domains` | Attach custom domain, return required DNS records |
| `GET /v1/sites/{id}/domains/{d}` | DNS verification + cert state |
| `POST /v1/sites/{id}/suspend` | Payment failure / abuse |
| `DELETE /v1/sites/{id}` | Teardown after grace period |

Every mutating call takes an idempotency key. DNS, ACME, and registrar operations are slow and fail halfway, so these are jobs, not synchronous requests — Kodely fires the call, gets a job ID, and polls or takes a webhook.

## TLS for thousands of custom domains

This is the part people underestimate, and Caddy solves it almost entirely:

- **Wildcard cert for `*.kodely.app`** via DNS-01. One cert covers every default subdomain.
- **Custom domains via Caddy's on-demand TLS.** Caddy issues a cert on the *first HTTPS request* for an unknown hostname, but only after calling your `ask` endpoint. That endpoint hits Kodely: "is `acme-bakery.com` attached to an active, paid site?" Yes → cert issued automatically. No → connection refused, no cert.

That endpoint must be fast, cached, and rate-limited — it's on the TLS handshake path, and without limits anyone can point a hostname at your IP and make you hammer Let's Encrypt until you hit rate limits.

## Custom domains — two products, don't conflate them

**Bring your own domain** (build first, it's much simpler):
- Subdomain → `CNAME` to `sites.kodely.app`
- Apex → `A` record to your anycast IP, since apex CNAMEs are invalid. Show both records in the UI and detect which case they're in.
- Ownership proof via a `TXT` at `_kodely-verify.{domain}` before you'll serve it — otherwise someone attaches a domain they don't own.

**Sell the domain in-app** — a genuinely bigger lift, because you're becoming a registrar reseller:
- **Namecheap or Porkbun** for MVP (free API, low friction). **OpenSRS/Tucows or Enom** when volume justifies it — better margins, real reseller tooling.
- You inherit: TLD-by-TLD pricing and markup, RDAP/WHOIS contact collection, **ICANN registrant email verification** (domain gets suspended if the customer ignores it), auto-renew, the 60-day post-registration transfer lock, and the fact that **domains are non-refundable the moment they're registered** — charge before you register, and make the no-refund term explicit at checkout or you'll eat chargebacks.
- Decide now whether the customer or Nxeon is registrant of record. Make it the customer. Being registrant on thousands of domains you don't control is a liability, and it makes leaving feel like a hostage situation.
- You'll also need authoritative DNS. PowerDNS on Nxeon with its HTTP API is the self-hosted path; Cloudflare's API is the zero-ops one.

## Data model on the Kodely side

`Site`, `Deployment`, `Domain`, `Certificate`, `Subscription`, plus a `ProvisioningJob` table. Domains need an explicit state machine — `pending_dns → verifying → cert_pending → live`, with `failed` and `suspended` — because customers will add the CNAME three days later and the UI has to explain exactly where they're stuck.

Run a reconciliation loop that compares Kodely's DB against Nxeon's actual state. They *will* drift.

## Two things worth planning for now

**Abuse.** An AI site generator with free hosting is a phishing kit. You'll get sites impersonating banks on your IP ranges, and the consequences land on Nxeon's IP reputation and abuse desk, not on the customer. Budget for: a content scan on deploy, a `abuse@` path, one-click suspend, and separate IP ranges for free-tier vs paid so a burst of free-tier abuse can't blackhole your paying customers.

**Billing coupling.** Hosting is a monthly Stripe subscription you can cancel cleanly. A domain is a yearly, non-refundable, externally-billed obligation. Keep them as separate line items with separate lifecycles — if someone cancels hosting, their domain doesn't evaporate.

## Suggested order

1. Shared edge + `*.kodely.app` subdomains — every generated site gets a live URL. Ship this alone and it's already a real feature.
2. Bring-your-own-domain with on-demand TLS.
3. Stripe tiers + suspend-on-failure.

The Name.com CORE API is a RESTful interface enabling developers to "search, register, and manage domains, DNS records, WHOIS privacy, and more" through secure HTTP requests.

- **Production:** `https://api.name.com`
- **Sandbox:** `https://api.dev.name.com`

The API uses HTTP Basic Authentication with your username and API token (not your account password). Sandbox environments require appending "-test" to your username.

- Domain searching and availability checks
- Domain registration
- DNS record management
- URL forwarding
- Vanity nameservers
- Webhook notifications
- Domain transfers

Yes—a fully separated testing environment exists with preloaded testing credit, allowing safe experimentation without real charges or production impact.

The v4 API remains supported but is **not yet deprecated**. The documentation states it will "sunset at a predetermined time in 2026."
